opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most exciting aspects of where robotics is heading, and it's something that I feel is underappreciated. The way we usually think about training robots is that you collect a big dataset, you train a model, and then you deploy it, and that's kind of the end of the story. But that's not how people learn. When you start a new job, you don't show up already knowing everything. You have some general background knowledge, some common sense, and then you learn on the job, often with the help of people who are around you.

So with robots, once you have a foundation model that has enough general competence to do something reasonable, maybe not perfectly, but reasonably, then you can put it into a setting where it's actually doing useful work, and the people around it can help it improve. That help can take a lot of different forms. Sometimes it's a person stepping in and correcting a mistake, kind of like an intervention, where the robot is about to do something wrong and the person shows it what to do instead. Sometimes it's just feedback, saying "that was good" or "that wasn't quite right." And increasingly it can be natural language, where someone just tells the robot, "no, put the cup on the other side," or "be more careful with that." Because these models are built on top of vision-language models, they can actually understand that kind of instruction and incorporate it.

And the really important thing is that this creates a flywheel. The robot is doing real work, so it's generating real experience in the actual deployment distribution, which is exactly the data you want. And it's learning from its own mistakes, which is something you just can't get from demonstrations alone. When you only train on demonstrations, the robot never sees what happens when things go wrong, so it doesn't know how to recover. But when it's out there doing the task and someone helps it out of a bad situation, that's incredibly valuable data.

We've seen in our own work that combining this kind of human correction with reinforcement learning can take a policy that's, say, decent and make it really robust and fast, to the point where it can do a task reliably for hours. And I think long-term, the vision is that robots get deployed, they're useful from the start, but they keep getting better, and the more of them there are out in the world, the more they learn collectively. Humans in the loop are the thing that makes that bootstrapping possible, because they provide the safety net and the guidance while the robot is still getting there.

r001.rationale: The response says that once a robot has reasonable competence, people can guide it with natural-language task instructions, which it can incorporate to improve.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says robots learn from people’s feedback and corrections while doing real work.

r003.rationale: It connects a foundation model’s general competence and vision-language models to the robot’s ability to understand and incorporate human instructions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important questions for the next few years, and I'll try to explain why I think that.

The thing about robots that's different from, say, language models is that for a language model, the data was just already there. People wrote the internet, and then you train on it. For robots, there's no internet of robot experience. Someone has to go out and collect it, and right now that's expensive. You have people teleoperating robots, doing demonstrations, and that works, it's how we bootstrap these systems, but it doesn't scale the way you'd want it to.

So the question is, where does the data come from at scale? And I think the answer is that it comes from deployment. The robot has to be doing something useful, and in the course of doing that useful thing, it's getting experience, and that experience makes it better. That's the flywheel. And the reason humans matter in that loop is that the robot, at least initially, is not going to be good enough to be left alone. It's going to make mistakes. And the question is what happens when it makes a mistake.

If you have a person there, that person can intervene. They can correct it, they can take over for a second and then hand control back. And every one of those interventions is actually an incredibly informative signal. It's telling you not just "this was wrong," which is what you'd get from a sparse reward, but "here's what you should have done instead, in exactly the situation where you were confused." That's way more information per unit of time than you get from a robot flailing around on its own trying to discover things from scratch.

We've actually seen this in our own work. If you have a policy that's maybe seventy, eighty percent reliable and you deploy it with a person who corrects the failures, and you train on both the autonomous successes and the corrections, you can get to a very high success rate really quickly, way faster than if you'd just collected more demonstrations up front. Because the corrections are targeted at the stuff the robot is actually bad at, rather than the stuff that's easy.

And there's a second piece to this that I think people underappreciate, which is that a human in the loop also lets you be much more aggressive about what you try. If the robot is alone, you have to be really conservative, because a mistake might break something. If there's a person there who can catch it, you can let it explore, let it try things it's uncertain about. And that's where a lot of the learning actually happens.

Now, the long-term vision is that the amount of supervision goes down over time. In the beginning maybe you need one person per robot. Then one person watching ten robots. Then one person watching a hundred, and they only step in once in a while. And at that point you've basically got a system that's accumulating experience across an entire fleet, and every correction anywhere improves all of them. That's the thing that I think would really change the picture, where robot learning stops being bottlenecked on data collection and starts looking more like something that just gets better the more it's used.

r001.rationale: The response describes people correcting or taking over from a robot, but does not say that spoken task instructions supervise a sufficiently competent robot.

r002.rationale: It says human interventions and corrections during deployment provide informative feedback that helps the robot improve.

r003.rationale: It contrasts language-model training data with robot experience but does not claim that prior knowledge from large models helps robots understand collaborative interactions.

astra-6.text:
I think the big opportunity is that humans can help robots get through situations where they would otherwise get stuck. Imagine a robot working in a kitchen. It can do most of a task, but then it encounters a drawer it doesn’t know how to open. A person helps it with that step, and then the robot continues. That intervention is also training data. If the learning system is set up correctly, the robot should become less dependent on that help over time.

What makes this interesting is that the robot’s own experience tells you where you need more data. You don’t have to anticipate every possible difficulty and demonstrate it in advance. You deploy the robot with some initial capability, it encounters the limits of that capability, and people provide guidance precisely at those limits.

The hard part is making that interaction useful for learning without making it burdensome for the person. If you have to supervise the robot constantly, it’s probably easier to do the task yourself. But if a brief intervention lets it finish the job and improves its behavior the next time, then you have a potentially very powerful way to keep learning after deployment.

r001.rationale: The response says people can intervene to help a robot and that the intervention can serve as training data, but it does not specify spoken task instructions or tie them to a robot with sufficient competence.

r002.rationale: It says people provide guidance during work when the robot reaches its limits, and that the robot can learn from those interventions and improve its behavior next time.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention prior knowledge from large models or say that such knowledge helps robots understand collaborative interactions.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to think about this is that humans can provide both examples and corrections. If a robot is working alongside a person, it can observe how they do the task, try parts of it itself, and get help when it encounters something it doesn’t understand.

The interesting challenge is making that help useful beyond the immediate situation. Suppose the robot is trying to put something away and gets stuck. A person intervenes and shows it what to do. You’d like that intervention to become training data, so the next time it encounters a similar situation, it can handle it on its own.

That could create a useful feedback loop: the robot does the things it already knows how to do, people help with the difficult cases, and those difficult cases are precisely where it gets new experience. But the robot also has to recognize when it needs help. If it confidently makes mistakes, or asks a person about every little thing, it’s going to be a pretty frustrating coworker.

r001.rationale: The response discusses observing a person and receiving help, but does not state that spoken task instructions provide supervision once the robot has sufficient competence.

r002.rationale: It says robots can learn from people’s examples and corrections during collaboration, including interventions that become training data for similar situations.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention large models or prior knowledge from them enabling robots to understand collaborative interactions.
